blocks.content: SQL HAVING covered filtering grouped results by their own aggregate values, but it never actually explained what those aggregate values are or how they get computed. Aggregate Functions fills that gap directly, covering the actual functions, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX, that GROUP BY and HAVING genuinely rely on to summarize a group of rows.

This topic covers what each of the five genuinely common aggregate functions actually computes, how they behave with or without GROUP BY, a specific and genuinely important detail about how they treat NULL values, and how multiple aggregates can appear together in one single query.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035550052-241290128.png

blocks.content: 1. The Five Genuinely Common Aggregate Functions
blocks.text: 1. The Five Genuinely Common Aggregate Functions

blocks.content: COUNT returns how many rows are present, either in the entire table or within each group. SUM returns the total of a numeric column, adding every value in the relevant group together. AVG returns the average of a numeric column, the sum divided by the count.

MIN returns the smallest value present in a column, and MAX returns the largest. Together, these five functions cover the genuine large majority of real, everyday aggregation needs in actual SQL queries.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035551965-722610657.png
blocks.alt: The five common aggregate functions: COUNT for how many rows, SUM for a total, AVG for an average, MIN for the smallest value, and MAX for the largest

2. Without GROUP BY Versus With GROUP BY
blocks.text: 2. Without GROUP BY Versus With GROUP BY

blocks.content: An aggregate function used with no GROUP BY clause at all genuinely summarizes the entire table into a single row, treating every row in the table as one big implicit group.

An aggregate function used alongside GROUP BY genuinely summarizes each defined group into its own separate row instead, computing that same aggregate independently for every distinct group that GROUP BY actually produces.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035553596-340793946.png
blocks.alt: An aggregate function with no GROUP BY summarizes the entire table into one row; an aggregate alongside GROUP BY summarizes each group into its own row

blocks.content: 3. A Worked Example
A concrete query shows several aggregate functions applied together, with no GROUP BY, to summarize an entire table into one row.
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(amount) FROM orders;
blocks.code: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(amount) FROM orders;

codes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(amount) FROM orders;

blocks.content: This query returns a single row containing the total number of orders, the total revenue across every order, and the average order value, all computed from the entire orders table at once, since no GROUP BY clause was included.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035555096-717230957.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: an orders table summarized with COUNT, SUM, and AVG together into one row, no GROUP BY involved

blocks.content: 4. How Aggregate Functions Genuinely Treat NULL
blocks.text: 4. How Aggregate Functions Genuinely Treat NULL

blocks.content: SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX all genuinely ignore NULL values entirely when computing their result, a NULL value in the relevant column simply does not participate in the calculation at all, as though that row was not there for the purpose of that specific aggregate.

COUNT with a specific column name also genuinely ignores NULL values in that column, but COUNT star counts every single row regardless of whether any column actually contains NULL, since it is counting rows, not evaluating a specific column value.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035556613-754946009.png
blocks.alt: SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX genuinely ignore NULL values; COUNT with a column name ignores NULL too, but COUNT star counts every row regardless

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Assuming AVG treats a NULL value as zero when computing an average. It genuinely does not, NULL values are excluded entirely from both the sum and the count used to compute that average, which can meaningfully change the result compared to treating NULL as zero.
5. Combining Aggregate Functions With GROUP BY
blocks.text: 5. Combining Aggregate Functions With GROUP BY

blocks.content: Aggregate functions combined with GROUP BY genuinely compute one independent result per group, not one single result across the whole table. Multiple different aggregate functions can genuinely appear together in the same query too.

This query returns one row per department, each with its own employee count and its own average salary, computed entirely independently for every department, since GROUP BY ensures each aggregate function genuinely operates on only that department own rows.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035558170-406667843.png
blocks.alt: Aggregate functions combined with GROUP BY compute one independent result per group, and multiple different aggregates can appear in the same query

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Every aggregate function in a query alongside GROUP BY genuinely computes its own value per group, independently. There is no shared state between what COUNT computes for one group and what AVG computes for that same group beyond both operating on the same underlying rows.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine aggregate function usage. Assuming AVG treats NULL values as zero, which genuinely changes the actual computed average compared to how AVG genuinely behaves. Selecting a non aggregated, non grouped column without a genuine GROUP BY clause present, which is genuinely ambiguous, covered directly in the earlier GROUP BY topic.

And confusing which specific function actually fits a given real question, reaching for SUM when the actual question genuinely calls for AVG, or reaching for COUNT when the question genuinely needs SUM instead.

blocks.alt: Common mistakes: assuming AVG treats NULL as zero, selecting an ungrouped column without GROUP BY, and confusing which aggregate function actually fits the question

Mixing an aggregated column with a non aggregated, non grouped one: genuinely ambiguous, requires GROUP BY to be well defined.
Picking the wrong function for the actual question: confirm whether you genuinely need a total, an average, or a simple count first.
